modules.title: Introduction to Animal Nutrition and Classes of Nutrients
modules.html:
Introduction to Animal Nutrition

Animal nutrition is the branch of agricultural science concerned with the study of feed, its nutrient composition, and how these nutrients are utilised by the animal body for maintenance, growth, reproduction and production of meat, milk, eggs and other products. Proper nutrition is the single most important factor influencing productivity and profitability in livestock enterprises, since feed alone can account for up to 70% of total production cost.

An animal requires nutrients for several life processes: maintenance of normal body functions and temperature, growth of new tissues, reproduction, and production of economic products such as milk, meat, eggs and wool. Nutrients are supplied through feed, which must contain the correct balance of carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water to meet the physiological needs of the animal at different stages of its life.

Basic Concepts in Animal Nutrition

  • Nutrient: any chemical substance in feed that nourishes the body.
  • Ration: the total amount of feed given to an animal in 24 hours.
  • Balanced ration: a ration that supplies all required nutrients in the correct proportion and amount needed by the animal.
  • Maintenance requirement: the amount of nutrients needed just to keep the animal alive and in a stable condition without gain or loss in body weight.
  • Production requirement: the additional nutrients needed above maintenance for growth, pregnancy, lactation or egg production.

Classes of Nutrients and Their Functions

Nutrient ClassMain FunctionExample Sources
CarbohydratesProvide energy; excess stored as fatMaize, cassava, guinea corn
ProteinsGrowth and repair of body tissuesGroundnut cake, soybean meal, fishmeal
Fats and oilsConcentrated energy source; carry fat-soluble vitaminsPalm oil, vegetable oil
VitaminsRegulate body processes; prevent deficiency diseasesGreen vegetables, fish liver oil
MineralsBone formation, enzyme activity, nerve functionBone meal, oyster shell, salt
WaterSolvent, transport medium, temperature regulationDrinking water, moisture in feed

Importance of Good Nutrition

  1. It ensures optimum growth rate and body development.
  2. It improves reproductive efficiency and fertility.
  3. It increases production of milk, eggs and meat.
  4. It boosts the animal's resistance to diseases.
  5. It reduces cost of production when rations are formulated efficiently using locally available feed ingredients.

A farmer who understands the principles of nutrition can select and combine feed ingredients to produce cost-effective and balanced rations, thereby maximising productivity while minimising feed wastage and cost.

examples.a: A ration is the total quantity of feed given to an animal in a 24-hour period. A balanced ration is a ration that supplies all the nutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water) required by an animal in the correct proportion and quantity for maintenance and production.

examples.q: A farmer notices that his growing pigs have weak, poorly developed bones. Which class of nutrient is most likely deficient, and why?
examples.a: Minerals, specifically calcium and phosphorus (and possibly Vitamin D which aids their absorption), are most likely deficient. These minerals are essential for bone formation and mineralisation; their deficiency leads to weak bones, a condition known as rickets in young animals.

modules.title: Feed Classification, Digestibility and Feed Conversion Ratio
modules.html:
Feed Classification, Digestibility and Feed Conversion Ratio

Feeds are broadly classified into roughages and concentrates. Roughages are bulky feeds high in fibre and low in energy, such as grasses, legumes, hay and silage, commonly fed to ruminants. Concentrates are feeds low in fibre and high in energy or protein, such as maize, groundnut cake and fishmeal, fed to both monogastric and ruminant animals. Concentrates are further divided into energy concentrates (e.g. maize, cassava) and protein concentrates (e.g. soybean meal, fishmeal).

Digestibility refers to the proportion of feed nutrients that are absorbed into the body rather than excreted in faeces. It is usually expressed as a percentage and calculated using the formula:

$$ \text{Digestibility (\%)} = \frac{\text{Nutrient intake} - \text{Nutrient in faeces}}{\text{Nutrient intake}} \times 100 $$

A key performance index in livestock feeding, especially in poultry and pig production, is the Feed Conversion Ratio (FCR), which measures how efficiently an animal converts feed into body weight gain. It is given by:

$$ FCR = \frac{\text{Total feed intake (kg)}}{\text{Total weight gain (kg)}} $$

A lower FCR indicates higher feed efficiency, meaning the animal converts less feed into a unit of weight gain, which is economically desirable.

Worked Illustration of FCR

Suppose a broiler chicken consumed 4 kg of feed over six weeks and gained 2 kg in body weight during that period. Then:

$$ FCR = \frac{4\ \text{kg}}{2\ \text{kg}} = 2.0 $$

This means 2 kg of feed was required to produce 1 kg of body weight gain, which is a good FCR value for broilers.

Factors Affecting Digestibility and FCR

  • Age and species of the animal.
  • Quality and composition of the feed (high fibre content reduces digestibility).
  • Level of feeding and feed processing method.
  • Health status and presence of parasites.
  • Environmental conditions such as temperature and stress.

Comparing Roughages and Concentrates

FeatureRoughageConcentrate
Fibre contentHigh (over 18%)Low
Energy densityLowHigh
ExampleElephant grass, hayMaize, fishmeal

Farmers use FCR values to compare the economic efficiency of different feeds, breeds or feeding strategies, choosing options that give the lowest FCR at the lowest cost.

examples.q: A pig consumed 60 kg of feed over a period and gained 20 kg in body weight. Calculate the feed conversion ratio (FCR) and comment on the result.
examples.a: Using $$ FCR = \frac{\text{Total feed intake}}{\text{Total weight gain}} = \frac{60\ \text{kg}}{20\ \text{kg}} = 3.0 $$ This means 3 kg of feed was needed to produce 1 kg of weight gain. This FCR is higher (less efficient) than the broiler's FCR of 2.0, since pigs generally have higher FCR values than poultry.

examples.q: An animal was fed a ration containing 8 kg of a particular nutrient, and 2 kg of that nutrient was recovered in the faeces. Calculate the digestibility of the nutrient.
examples.a: Using $$ \text{Digestibility (\%)} = \frac{\text{Nutrient intake} - \text{Nutrient in faeces}}{\text{Nutrient intake}} \times 100 = \frac{8 - 2}{8} \times 100 = 75\% $$ Therefore 75% of the nutrient consumed was digested and absorbed by the animal.

modules.title: Principles of Ration Formulation and Pearson's Square Method
modules.html:
Principles of Ration Formulation and the Pearson's Square Method

Ration formulation is the process of combining two or more feed ingredients in appropriate proportions to produce a balanced diet that meets the nutrient requirements of a given class of livestock. The nutrient most commonly balanced through formulation is crude protein (CP), although energy, calcium and phosphorus levels are also considered in commercial practice. The ration must meet the nutrient requirement of the target animal, use available and affordable ingredients, be free of toxins, and balance energy and protein sources appropriately.

The Pearson's Square Method (Two Ingredients)

The Pearson's Square is a simple arithmetic technique used to determine the proportion of two feed ingredients required to obtain a mixture with a desired nutrient percentage. The desired percentage is placed at the centre of a square, while the percentages of the two ingredients are placed at the top-left and bottom-left corners. Diagonal subtraction (ignoring sign) gives the parts of each ingredient required.

Worked Example: Formulate a ration containing 18% crude protein (CP) using maize (9% CP) and groundnut cake, GNC (45% CP).

  1. Parts of Maize $$ = 45 - 18 = 27 \text{ parts} $$
  2. Parts of GNC $$ = 18 - 9 = 9 \text{ parts} $$
  3. Total parts $$ = 27 + 9 = 36 \text{ parts} $$

$$ \%\ \text{Maize} = \frac{27}{36} \times 100 = 75\% \qquad \%\ \text{GNC} = \frac{9}{36} \times 100 = 25\% $$

So, mixing 75 kg of maize with 25 kg of GNC per 100 kg of feed gives a ration with 18% crude protein. Check: $$ (0.75 \times 9) + (0.25 \times 45) = 6.75 + 11.25 = 18\% $$, confirming the answer is correct.

Two-Stage Ration Formulation with Four Ingredients

In practice, rations often contain more than two ingredients. Ingredients are first grouped into an energy group and a protein group; a combined (average) CP value is found for each group, and the Pearson's Square is then applied between the two group averages. This is called two-stage formulation.

Problem: Formulate 100 kg of a 20% CP ration using an energy group of maize (9% CP) and cassava meal (2% CP) mixed in equal parts (50:50), and a protein group of GNC (45% CP) and fishmeal (60% CP) mixed in equal parts (50:50).

Stage 1 – average CP of each group:

$$ \text{Energy group CP} = \frac{9 + 2}{2} = 5.5\% \qquad \text{Protein group CP} = \frac{45 + 60}{2} = 52.5\% $$

Stage 2 – Pearson's Square between the group averages to hit 20% CP:

$$ \text{Parts of Energy group} = 52.5 - 20 = 32.5 \qquad \text{Parts of Protein group} = 20 - 5.5 = 14.5 $$

$$ \text{Total parts} = 32.5 + 14.5 = 47 $$

$$ \%\ \text{Energy group} = \frac{32.5}{47} \times 100 \approx 69.15\% \qquad \%\ \text{Protein group} = \frac{14.5}{47} \times 100 \approx 30.85\% $$

In 100 kg feed: Energy group = 69.15 kg, split equally into 34.57 kg maize and 34.57 kg cassava meal; Protein group = 30.85 kg, split equally into 15.43 kg GNC and 15.43 kg fishmeal. Check: $$ (0.6915 \times 5.5) + (0.3085 \times 52.5) \approx 3.80 + 16.20 = 20\% $$, confirming the four-ingredient ration meets the 20% CP target.

examples.q: Using the Pearson's Square, formulate a ration containing 16% crude protein using maize (8% CP) and soybean meal (44% CP). Find the percentage of each ingredient needed per 100 kg of feed.
examples.a: Parts of maize $$= 44 - 16 = 28$$; Parts of soybean meal $$= 16 - 8 = 8$$; Total parts $$= 28+8=36$$. % Maize $$= \frac{28}{36}\times100 \approx 77.78\%$$. % Soybean meal $$= \frac{8}{36}\times100 \approx 22.22\%$$. So per 100 kg feed, mix about 77.78 kg maize with 22.22 kg soybean meal. Check: $$(0.7778\times8)+(0.2222\times44)\approx 6.22+9.78=16\%$$.

examples.q: Using two-stage formulation, formulate 100 kg of a 22% CP ration using an energy group of maize (9% CP) and rice bran (12% CP) in equal parts, and a protein group of GNC (45% CP) and blood meal (80% CP) in equal parts.
examples.a: Stage 1: Energy group CP $$= \frac{9+12}{2}=10.5\%$$; Protein group CP $$= \frac{45+80}{2}=62.5\%$$. Stage 2: Parts of energy group $$=62.5-22=40.5$$; Parts of protein group $$=22-10.5=11.5$$; Total $$=40.5+11.5=52$$. % Energy group $$=\frac{40.5}{52}\times100\approx77.88\%$$; % Protein group $$=\frac{11.5}{52}\times100\approx22.12\%$$. Per 100 kg: Energy group = 77.88 kg (38.94 kg maize + 38.94 kg rice bran); Protein group = 22.12 kg (11.06 kg GNC + 11.06 kg blood meal). Check: $$(0.7788\times10.5)+(0.2212\times62.5)\approx 8.18+13.83=22\%$$.

quiz.q: Which of the following is the main function of carbohydrates in an animal's body?
quiz.solution: Carbohydrates are the main energy-providing nutrient class; excess carbohydrate is stored as body fat, while proteins are responsible for tissue growth and antibody formation.

quiz.q: The formula for Feed Conversion Ratio (FCR) is:
options: Weight gain divided by feed intake
Feed intake divided by weight gain
Feed intake multiplied by weight gain
quiz.solution: FCR = Total feed intake (kg) / Total weight gain (kg). It measures how much feed is required to produce one unit of weight gain.

quiz.q: A broiler consumed 5 kg of feed and gained 2.5 kg in weight. What is its FCR?
Using the Pearson's Square to obtain 20% CP from maize (10% CP) and fishmeal (60% CP), what percentage of maize is required?
quiz.solution: Parts of maize = 60 - 20 = 40; parts of fishmeal = 20 - 10 = 10; total = 50. % maize = 40/50 x 100 = 80%.

quiz.q: Which of these feeds is classified as a roughage?
quiz.solution: Elephant grass is bulky and high in fibre, making it a roughage. Maize, fishmeal and groundnut cake are concentrates.

quiz.q: Digestibility of a nutrient is calculated as:
options: Nutrient in faeces divided by nutrient intake
Nutrient intake minus nutrient in faeces, divided by nutrient intake, times 100
Nutrient intake divided by nutrient in faeces
Nutrient intake plus nutrient in faeces
quiz.solution: Digestibility (%) = (Nutrient intake - Nutrient in faeces) / Nutrient intake x 100.

quiz.q: An animal was fed 10 kg of a nutrient and excreted 4 kg in faeces. What is the digestibility percentage?
In two-stage ration formulation, ingredients are first grouped into:
quiz.solution: In two-stage formulation, ingredients are grouped into an energy group and a protein group; each group's average CP is found before applying the Pearson's Square.

quiz.q: Which nutrient class is required in the largest amount by the animal body and serves as a solvent and transport medium?
quiz.solution: Water is required in the largest quantity and functions as a solvent, transport medium and in temperature regulation, though it is often overlooked as a nutrient.

quiz.q: Which of these is a protein concentrate?
quiz.solution: Soybean meal is high in protein and is classified as a protein concentrate; maize, cassava meal and guinea corn are energy concentrates.

quiz.q: A lower feed conversion ratio (FCR) indicates:
quiz.solution: A lower FCR means less feed is required to produce a unit of weight gain, indicating higher feed efficiency, which is economically desirable.

quiz.q: To formulate a 24% CP ration using an energy group of average CP 8% and a protein group of average CP 54%, how many total parts are obtained using Pearson's Square?
quiz.solution: Parts of energy group = 54-24=30; parts of protein group = 24-8=16; total parts = 30+16=46.

quiz.q: Which of the following best defines a ration?
options: Feed given to an animal over one week
Total feed given to an animal in 24 hours
Amount of water an animal drinks daily
quiz.solution: A ration is defined as the total quantity of feed given to an animal within a 24-hour period.

quiz.q: Which vitamin group requires fat for absorption and includes vitamins A, D, E and K?
quiz.solution: Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble vitamins, requiring dietary fat for proper absorption, unlike water-soluble vitamins such as B-complex and C.

quiz.q: In formulating a ration to contain 15% CP using maize (5% CP) and fishmeal (65% CP), what is the percentage of fishmeal required?
quiz.solution: Parts of maize = 65-15=50; parts of fishmeal = 15-5=10; total=60. % fishmeal = 10/60 x100 = 16.67%.
